06 · From the NAO to winter extremes¶

Question for this notebook. In the real world, a positive winter NAO brings stronger westerly winds: milder and wetter weather to northern Europe, drier weather to the south. Do the two EERIE models reproduce that link for winter extremes (the wettest day, the rain on very wet days, the mildest day), with the right sign, pattern and strength?

This is the centrepiece of the project: it connects the large-scale circulation (notebook 04) to the regional extremes (notebook 05).

Data. 29 winters, 1986–2014 (the winters that have daily data).

  • NAO index per winter, from notebook 04.
  • Winter RX1day, winter R95p and winter TXx at every grid cell, from notebook 05.
  • Four datasets: ERA5 (reanalysis reference), E-OBS (station-based, land only), ICON-ESM-ER and IFS-FESOM2-SR.

Which NAO goes with which extremes. Each model's extremes are related to that model's own NAO winters. ERA5 and E-OBS extremes are both related to the ERA5 NAO, because they describe the same real winters.

Method (fixed in docs/methods.md before any result was produced):

  1. Remove the straight-line trend from both the NAO index and the extreme index, so that a shared long-term drift (for example warming) cannot masquerade as an NAO effect.
  2. At every grid cell, compute the correlation with the NAO and the regression slope: the change in the extreme index per one standard deviation of NAO.
  3. Test each cell (two-sided t-test) and then apply false-discovery-rate control across all cells, so that the map is not littered with chance "significant" dots.
  4. As a simpler cross-check, compare the ten most positive with the ten most negative NAO winters.

The NAO index used. Notebook 04 showed that ICON-ESM-ER's own leading pressure pattern is a mixture and not a clean NAO. So the main analysis measures every dataset along the same pattern, the ERA5 NAO pattern, in units of the ERA5 standard deviation. Section 8 repeats the key numbers with two other index definitions to show how much the choice matters.

Background: the terms used in this notebook¶

If you know these already, skip to section 1.

Term What it means here
Correlation (r) How consistently two things vary together from winter to winter, from −1 to +1. r = +0.6 between NAO and RX1day at a place means wet-extreme winters there tend to be positive-NAO winters. It says nothing about how big the effect is.
Regression slope How big the effect is: the change in the extreme index for a one-standard-deviation increase in the NAO. For example "+4 mm per SD".
Per 1 SD of NAO One standard deviation of the ERA5 winter NAO index, the same yardstick for every dataset. A typical positive winter is about +1 SD.
Detrending Subtracting the best-fit straight line over 1986–2014 from each series before correlating them.
p value The probability of seeing a correlation at least this strong purely by chance if there were no real link. Small is convincing; below 0.05 is the usual threshold.
Multiple testing A map has thousands of grid cells. Testing each at the 5% level would flag about 5% of them even if the NAO had no effect anywhere.
False-discovery-rate (FDR) control A standard correction for that problem (Benjamini–Hochberg; recommended for climate maps by Wilks 2016). It raises the bar so that, among the cells finally marked, only a small expected share (here 10%) are false alarms. Dots on the maps mark cells that pass it.
Composite The average over a group of winters. "NAO+ minus NAO−" is the average of the ten most positive winters minus the average of the ten most negative.
Bootstrap interval An uncertainty range obtained by re-drawing the winters many times at random. If the range excludes zero, the difference is unlikely to be chance.
Pattern correlation How similar the shapes of two maps are, from −1 to 1. Used here to ask: does the model's NAO-response map look like the reference's?

How to read the maps. All maps in this notebook show a response to the NAO. Orange means the index goes up in positive-NAO winters, blue means it goes down, grey means no link. Small dots mark grid cells where the link passes the significance test with FDR control. All panels of one figure share one colour scale. E-OBS is blank over sea.

Colours of the points and lines. Dark grey ERA5, light grey E-OBS, blue ICON-ESM-ER, orange IFS-FESOM2-SR.

1. Setup¶

What this cell does. Loads the project code. The statistics are in eerie_uk/relationships.py; each function has a unit test on synthetic data where the true answer is known.

In [1]:
import sys, warnings
sys.path.insert(0, '../src')
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
from pathlib import Path
from eerie_uk import climatology as clim, extremes as ex, plotting, regions, relationships as rel, store

pd.set_option('display.width', 220, 'display.float_format', '{:.2f}'.format)
MODELS = ['icon-esm-er', 'ifs-fesom2-sr']
REFS = ['e-obs', 'era5']      # reference datasets
DATASETS = REFS + MODELS
NAO_OF = {'e-obs': 'era5', 'era5': 'era5', 'icon-esm-er': 'icon-esm-er', 'ifs-fesom2-sr': 'ifs-fesom2-sr'}
NAME = plotting.SOURCE_LABELS
WINTERS = (1986, 2014)

What this cell does. Loads the two inputs: the winter NAO indices saved by notebook 04 and the gridded winter extreme indices cached by notebook 05. E-OBS is put on the model grid, and a land mask is built for land-only statistics.

In [2]:
nao_table = pd.read_parquet('../app_assets/nao_index_winter.parquet')

def nao_index(source, column='nao_on_era5_pattern'):
    part = nao_table[(nao_table.source == source) & nao_table.year.between(*WINTERS)]
    return xr.DataArray(part[column].values, coords={'year': part.year.values}, dims='year')

indices = {d: ex.indices_for(d) for d in DATASETS}
grid = indices['icon-esm-er']
indices['e-obs'] = regions.to_grid(indices['e-obs'], grid)
land = regions.land_mask(grid.lat, grid.lon)

def winter_field(dataset, name):
    return indices[dataset][f'{name}_djf'].rename(year_djf='year')

print('winters:', WINTERS[0], 'to', WINTERS[1], '=', nao_index('era5').size)

winters: 1986 to 2014 = 29

2. Findings¶

29 winters, 1986–2014. One member per model. References for extremes: E-OBS (station-based, land) and ERA5 (reanalysis), both paired with the ERA5 NAO. All series detrended. "Per SD" means per one standard deviation of the ERA5 NAO.

UK and Ireland, land average: link between the winter NAO and winter extremes

E-OBS ERA5 ICON-ESM-ER IFS-FESOM2-SR
Wettest winter day (RX1day): correlation 0.56 0.32 0.28 0.57
… change per SD of NAO (95% range) +1.3 mm (0.6 to 2.1) +0.7 mm (−0.1 to 1.6) +1.6 mm (−0.6 to 3.9) +2.7 mm (1.2 to 4.3)
Very-wet-day rain (R95p): correlation 0.51 0.35 0.36 0.60
… change per SD of NAO (95% range) +10 mm (3 to 18) +6 mm (−0 to 13) +17 mm (−1 to 35) +17 mm (8 to 25)
Mildest winter day (TXx): correlation 0.32 0.31 0.21 0.12
Ten most positive minus ten most negative NAO winters, R95p +27 mm (11 to 43) see section 9 +20 mm (−1 to 41) +27 mm (8 to 45)

Bold: distinguishable from zero at the 5% level.

What this means, in plain words

  1. The real-world link is clear for rainfall extremes, but its strength over UK and Ireland depends on the reference. Both references agree on the sign. E-OBS gives correlations of about 0.5 (significant); ERA5 gives about 0.33 (not quite significant with 29 winters). In western Norway both references agree on a strong link (correlations 0.74 to 0.81). The two references' response maps resemble each other well (pattern correlation 0.72 to 0.83), so the regional pattern is clear even where the UK number is uncertain.
  2. Both models reproduce the textbook response of ordinary winter rainfall (Figure 1): wetter in the north, drier in the south in positive-NAO winters. This is the precondition for the rest.
  3. IFS-FESOM2-SR reproduces the NAO link to rainfall extremes: right sign, correlations over UK and Ireland (0.57 and 0.60) at the E-OBS end of the observed range, a response per SD as large as observed or larger, the right sign in western Norway and north-west France, and the closest response maps to both references (pattern correlation up to 0.74 with ERA5 for R95p).
  4. ICON-ESM-ER's link over UK and Ireland is weak (0.28 and 0.36), similar to ERA5's but below E-OBS's, so with two references it cannot be called wrong there. Two things are clearly off: its link in western Norway is weaker than in both references, and in north-west France it has the opposite sign to both references for very-wet-day rain (−0.46 against +0.28 to +0.34). In this model the dry side of the NAO reaches too far north (visible in Figure 1).
  5. The mildest winter day (TXx) shows a weak link over UK and Ireland in both references (0.31 to 0.32), and a clear one over Scandinavia that neither model reproduces (pattern correlations 0.17 to 0.30). Winter TXx is the least well captured of the three.
  6. Few model grid cells pass the FDR-controlled test, against 8–16% of land cells in each reference. A weaker NAO (standard deviation 0.52 and 0.78 of ERA5's in these winters) gives the models less signal to detect, so fewer dots is expected and is not by itself a fault.
  7. The choice of NAO index matters for ICON-ESM-ER and not for the others. With ICON-ESM-ER's own leading pattern its UK correlations vanish (0.02 and −0.06), confirming notebook 04: that pattern is not a clean NAO. For both references and IFS-FESOM2-SR all three definitions agree.

Answer to the question. IFS-FESOM2-SR reproduces the sign, the regional pattern and the strength of the observed NAO link to winter rainfall extremes. ICON-ESM-ER gets the sign right in the north, but its response is weaker in Norway and has the wrong sign in north-west France. Neither reproduces the link to the mildest winter day over Scandinavia. A lesson in its own right: over UK and Ireland the observed strength of the link differs between two good references, so "the observed value" is itself uncertain. With 29 winters and one member each these are indications, not established model properties.

3. The sample: 29 winters¶

Everything below rests on 29 winters per dataset. That is a small sample for a noisy link, and it is stated here once: with 29 winters and detrended series, a correlation needs to exceed about ±0.38 to pass an ordinary 5% test at a single place, and more than that after FDR control.

What this cell does. Describes the NAO sample of each dataset over these 29 winters: the spread of the index (in ERA5 standard deviations), and the index range of the ten most positive and ten most negative winters used later for composites.

In [3]:
rows = []
for s in ('era5',) + tuple(MODELS):
    series = nao_index(s).to_series()
    rows.append({'NAO from': NAME[s], 'winters': series.size, 'standard deviation': series.std(),
                 'most positive': series.max(), 'most negative': series.min(),
                 'mean of top 10': series.nlargest(10).mean(), 'mean of bottom 10': series.nsmallest(10).mean()})
pd.DataFrame(rows)

NAO from winters standard deviation most positive most negative mean of top 10 mean of bottom 10

1 ICON-ESM-ER 29 0.52 1.08 -1.15 0.65 -0.42
2 IFS-FESOM2-SR 29 0.78 1.68 -1.55 0.91 -0.75

Why the standard deviations differ. The index is in ERA5 units. A model whose NAO is weaker than ERA5's (notebook 04) has a standard deviation below 1 here. Its NAO winters are therefore less extreme, and the same slope per SD produces smaller winter-to-winter swings in that model.

4. Context: the NAO and ordinary winter rainfall¶

Before extremes, the textbook link: a positive NAO makes the whole winter wetter in the north and drier in the south. If a model does not show this, there is little point asking about extremes.

What this cell does. Regresses winter-mean precipitation (from the monthly data) on the NAO at every grid cell, for ERA5 and the two models. Dots mark cells that pass the FDR-controlled test.

In [4]:
context, context_mask = {}, {}
for s in ('era5',) + tuple(MODELS):
    winter_pr = clim.season_means(store.load(s, 'mon', 'pr', 'nw_europe'), 'DJF').sel(year=slice(*WINTERS))
    result = rel.correlate(winter_pr, nao_index(s))
    context[NAME[s]] = result.slope
    context_mask[NAME[s]] = rel.fdr_mask(result.p)
plotting.plot_field_panels(context, units='mm/day per +1 SD of NAO', diverging=True, stipple=context_mask,
                           title='Change in winter-mean precipitation per +1 SD of NAO, 1986-2014');

Figure 1. The response of ordinary winter rainfall to the NAO. Orange: wetter in positive-NAO winters; blue: drier. The expected picture is orange over Scotland, Norway and the northern seas and blue over Iberia and the Mediterranean, with the dividing line near 50°N.

What this cell does. Defines the function used for the three extreme indices below. For one index it computes, for each of the four datasets, the correlation map, the slope map and the FDR-significant cells, and collects summary numbers: the share of land cells that are significant and how closely each model's response map resembles each reference's (pattern correlation, land).

In [5]:
def analyse(name):
    out = {}
    for d in DATASETS:
        result = rel.correlate(winter_field(d, name), nao_index(NAO_OF[d]))
        result['significant'] = rel.fdr_mask(result.p)
        out[d] = result
    return out

def summarise(results):
    rows = []
    for d in DATASETS:
        r = results[d]
        row = {'dataset': NAME[d], 'land cells significant %': 100 * float(r.significant.where(land).mean()),
               'mean |r| over land': float(abs(r.r).where(land).mean())}
        for ref in REFS:
            both = land & r.slope.notnull() & results[ref].slope.notnull()
            row[f'pattern correlation with {NAME[ref]}'] = clim.pattern_stats(r.slope.where(both), results[ref].slope.where(both))['pattern correlation']
        rows.append(row)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

def maps(results, variable, units, title, limit=None):
    plotting.plot_field_panels({NAME[d]: results[d][variable] for d in DATASETS}, units=units, title=title, columns=2,
                               diverging=True, stipple={NAME[d]: results[d].significant for d in DATASETS}, limit=limit)

8. Regional numbers for UK and Ireland, and sensitivity to the index definition¶

What this cell does. Moves from maps to the headline region. It takes the land-average winter series saved by notebook 05 and, for each dataset and index, computes the correlation with the NAO, the slope per SD with its 95% range, and the p value. Western Norway and north-west France are included as supporting regions on the wet and dry sides of the NAO.

In [13]:
regional = pd.read_parquet('../app_assets/extremes_regional.parquet')
regional = regional[(regional.period == 'winter') & regional.year.between(*WINTERS)]
INDEX_LABELS = {'rx1day': 'RX1day (mm)', 'r95p': 'R95p (mm)', 'txx': 'TXx (°C)'}

def regional_link(column='nao_on_era5_pattern'):
    rows = []
    for region in regions.SUBREGIONS:
        for key, label in INDEX_LABELS.items():
            for d in DATASETS:
                part = regional[(regional.region == region) & (regional['index'] == key) & (regional.source == d)].sort_values('year')
                fit = rel.regress_series(part.value.values, nao_index(NAO_OF[d], column).sel(year=part.year.values).values)
                rows.append({'region': regions.LABELS[region], 'index': label, 'dataset': NAME[d], **fit})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

link = regional_link()
link[link.region == 'UK and Ireland'].drop(columns='region').reset_index(drop=True)

9. Positive against negative NAO winters¶

A simpler view that needs no straight-line assumption: the ten most positive NAO winters minus the ten most negative.

What this cell does. For UK and Ireland (land average), computes the difference in each winter extreme index between the ten most positive and the ten most negative NAO winters of each dataset, with a bootstrap 95% range.

In [17]:
rows = []
for key, label in INDEX_LABELS.items():
    for d in DATASETS:
        part = regional[(regional.region == 'uk_ireland') & (regional['index'] == key) & (regional.source == d)].sort_values('year')
        result = rel.composite_interval(part.value.values, nao_index(NAO_OF[d]).sel(year=part.year.values).values)
        rows.append({'index': label, 'dataset': NAME[d], 'NAO+ minus NAO-': result['difference'], 'low': result['low'], 'high': result['high'],
                     'range excludes zero': bool(result['low'] > 0 or result['high'] < 0)})
composites = pd.DataFrame(rows)
composites

11. Limitations¶

  • 29 winters and one member per model. This is the main limitation. A real but moderate link can easily fail to reach significance, and a model can differ from the reference by chance alone. Absence of dots is not evidence of absence of a link.
  • The models have a weaker NAO (notebook 04). Slopes are per ERA5 standard deviation, so they are comparable, but the model slopes are estimated from a narrower range of NAO values and are therefore less certain.
  • ICON-ESM-ER's mean state already resembles a strong positive NAO. Its response to further NAO swings is measured around that biased state.
  • Linear and simultaneous. The method assumes the response is proportional to the NAO and has the same size for positive and negative winters, and it looks only at the same winter.
  • Other drivers are ignored. Other circulation patterns (for example the East Atlantic pattern) also affect these extremes and can strengthen or mask the NAO signal.
  • RX1day is one day per winter, so it is the noisiest of the three indices.
  • FDR level 10%. A common choice for spatially correlated climate fields (Wilks 2016); a stricter level would mark fewer cells.
  • References. E-OBS smooths intense rain and covers land only; ERA5 rain is a model product.

12. Open questions¶

  1. Over UK and Ireland the two references disagree on the strength of the link (correlation 0.51 in E-OBS, 0.35 in ERA5). Which is closer to the truth, and why?
  2. Is ICON-ESM-ER's wrong-sign response over north-west France a consequence of its displaced NAO pattern (notebook 04)?
  3. With more members, would the models' links become significant over UK and Ireland? Notebook 08 shows how widely the link varies between identical runs.
